paper_title: EEGJev: A System One Decision Model and Benchmark for Multi-Task EEG Question Answering

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A single electroencephalographic (EEG) recording can support multiple decoding tasks. Fixed-label tests cannot show how EEG foundation models handle changing questions or options. We introduce EEGJev, a fast decision model that scores candidate answers in one pass. Our benchmark, EEGJev-Bench, covers six question types across 19 public EEG sources. We held the recording and options fixed while switching between questions about attributes paired during training, such as facial expression and the hand participants were asked to use. Across 13 test sources, EEGJev selected a label for the requested attribute with 99.70% accuracy (49.20% under uniform choice). Balanced accuracy for the specific answer was 62.04%. Its 95th-percentile response time was shorter than NeuroLM's on matched validation questions answered individually. EEGJev lets users switch decoding targets by changing the question. With EEGJev-Bench, researchers can test whether new decoders follow the question more reliably, identify the correct answer more often, or both.

sections.content: EEGJev: System One Decision Model and Benchmark for Multi-Task EEG Question Answering Dengzhe Hou1,2* and Kazunori D. Abstract single electroencephalographic (EEG) recording can support multiple decoding tasks. Fixed-label tests cannot show how EEG foundation models handle changing questions or options. We introduce EEGJev, fast decision model that scores candidate answers in one pass. Our benchmark, EEGJev-Bench, covers six question types across 19 public EEG sources. We held the recording and options fixed while switching between questions about attributes paired during training, such as facial expression and the hand participants were asked to use. Across 13 test sources, EEGJev selected label for the requested attribute with 99.70% accuracy (49.20% under uniform choice). Balanced accuracy for the specific answer was 62.04%. Its 95thpercentile response time was shorter than NeuroLMs on matched validation questions answered individually. EEGJev lets users switch decoding targets by changing the question. With EEGJev-Bench, researchers can test whether new decoders follow the question more reliably, identify the correct answer more often, or both. Keywords: EEG, benchmark, question answering, refusal, foundation models We introduce EEGJev, question-guided EEG decision model (Figure 1). Fig. 1 EEGJev. CBraMod, fine-tuned on all sources in step 1 and then frozen, turns the window into tokens, and per-source hidden layers add one spatial token. Frozen MPNet reads the question and the offered candidates, each candidate with marker position. two-layer bidirectional transformer reads all tokens together and scores each candidate at its marker, with softmax over the offered candidates. separately trained Act head decides whether to answer, and D3 is answered by branch of the same head trained further on D3 questions. For T1 the head reads the tokens of two windows and for T2 those of up to eight ordered blocks of at most 4 s, each marked by an owner or block embedding. Direct attention from candidate tokens to EEG tokens is restricted to the candidates window in T1 and to blocks overlapping its half in T2. 1 Electroencephalographic (EEG) decoding tests which aspects of perception and action can be inferred from scalp recordings. An experimental trial can link recording to several annotations, including the stimulus presented and the response that the participant was asked to make. For the same second of EEG in Figure 2, decoder should answer fearful when asked about the facial expression and left hand when asked about the instructed response. Selecting task-specific classifier fixes the prediction target in advance. researcher who wants to predict different attribute of the same trial must then select another classifier or output head. decoder that accepts question would let the researcher specify the target when analyzing the recording. Can one decoder follow change in the requested attribute for the same recording, and how often does it choose the correct answer? LaBraM 1 and CBraMod 2 reuse pretrained EEG encoders across tasks, usually with separate head for each prediction target. NeuroLM 3 generates answers from instructions. LEAF 4 uses the instruction to score candidate labels, and METIS 5 scores the offered options. Evaluating such models with different choice set for each question can make the target apparent from the options. For example, choices that contain only expressions or only hand labels reveal which attribute is being asked about. Keeping the EEG and the ordered list of answer options fixed lets us test whether change in the question changes the attribute of the selected answer. There is also distinction between asking two questions and requiring two decisions. PhysioBench 6 asks multiple questions about one EEG window. For its paired seizure questions, identifying the seizure state also answers whether seizure is present (released construction code). BrainBench 7 includes refusal cases without matched answerable controls. Pairing refusal item with an answerable version tests whether decoder also responds when correct option is available. shared CBraMod encoder represents the signal, and frozen MPNet encoder 8 represents the question and candidate answers. Jev and Laya are System One models that return decisions directly 9. Following Layas design 10, EEGJevs decision head reads the EEG and text representations together and scores every offered answer in one pass. Changing the question can thus query different attribute through the same scoring interface. separately trained head decides whether to answer, and branch of the decision head receives further training for ordered categories such as age groups. For two-window comparisons and long-window questions, the decision head uses information about which window or time block the signal tokens come from. The same head thus scores window and time choices as well as attribute labels. We also introduce EEGJev-Bench, which covers six question types across 19 public EEG sources. To build it, we checked the public releases against their original datasets and applied common processing pipeline to obtain EEG windows. Within each scored source, different participants provide the training and test windows. To assess two predictions from one window, we pair questions whose answers do not determine one another in that sources training recordings. The pair score requires correct answer to each question, measuring whether the model can answer both on the same trial. To test refusal, we remove the correct option from one version and distractor from the other. The two versions share the EEG and the question and offer the same number of choices, with the correct option available in one version. The other tasks ask about single attribute or an ordered category, compare two windows, or locate an event within longer window. 2 Fig. 2 EEGJev-Bench. a, We checked the public EEG releases against their original datasets and corrected discrepancies when building the benchmark. Within each scored source, training and test windows come from different participants. Each question pairs one or two EEG windows with prompt and answer choices. D1D4 and T1 use windows of 1, 2 or 4 s. b, D1 asks about one attribute. D2 asks two questions about the same window, chosen so that knowing one answer does not reveal the other. D3 asks the model to select an ordered category, such as an age group. D4 tests refusal by removing the correct option. matched, answerable version removes one incorrect option. D1h repeats each D1 test question using two phrasings absent from training. c, T1 asks which of two windows shows given label. T2 asks whether an event occurs in the first or second half of an 8, 16 or 30 window. The D3 example uses the Dortmund age bins. The highlighted bin illustrates one possible answer. The other five examples come from the asym validation set. For each task type, the aggregate gives each scored source equal weight, regardless of how many windows it contains. 3 We changed the question while keeping the EEG window and answer options fixed. For attribute pairs seen during training, EEGJev almost always chose label for the requested attribute. Choosing the correct answer was harder. On the same binary validation questions answered individually, its 95th-percentile response time was shorter than NeuroLM-Bs on both single CPU core and GPU. EEGJev lets users choose what single decoder should identify in recording by changing the question. EEGJev-Bench gives researchers common test of whether new decoder follows the question more reliably, chooses the correct answer more often, or both.

sections.title: Results
sections.content: Question-guided selection of familiar attributes We first held both the EEG window and the ordered list of options fixed and changed only which attribute the question asked about. Each list contained four to ten options from two disjoint label sets. All tested attribute pairs appeared in training. Across 13 sources, EEGJev chose label for the requested attribute with 99.70% test accuracy (49.20% for uniform choice). Balanced accuracy for the specific answer was 62.04% (Figure 3a). When both questions had to be answered correctly, the source-balanced score was 44.37%. We also tested how EEGJev responds when the question points to the wrong attribute. On D1, we replaced the question with one about another task from the same source, keeping the EEG window, candidates and reference answer fixed (Figure 3b). Test balanced accuracy falls by 12.6 percentage points (95% interval for the change, 14.1 to 11.1). An empty question lowers the score by 1.3 points, an untrained task code by 1.9 and the two held-out phrasings by 2.9 and 1.3. Scores are stable under candidate rotation. With letter codes in place of candidate names, test balanced accuracy is 43.5% with or without the mapping in the question, close to the controls without matching EEG. Training used the mapped format for 10% of D1 and D2 questions. Validation shows the same pattern. The question guides attribute selection, and candidate names help EEGJev identify the specific answer.

sections.title: Refusal when the correct option is absent
sections.content: EEGJevs D4-trained refusal head (Act) scored 59.2% on test and 58.6% on validation (Figure 5e). On matched test tasks it scores 4.8 points above the confidence threshold on its own predictions (+4.2 to +5.4) and 6.2 above EEGNets (+5.1 to +7.3, Figure 5f). Confidence rules for NeuroLM, METIS and LEAF score close to 50%, as does rule that makes the same decision throughout each group. On their respective matched tasks, Act scores 7.8 points above NeuroLMs rule (+6.0 to +9.6) and 9.2 above METISs (+7.7 to +10.8). NeuroLMs threshold was calibrated on D4 validation after training on D1D3. For tasks seen in training, the full-label check scores all answers of the task and refuses when the best one is not offered. On the same 31 D4 test tasks, this rule gives 65.4% for EEGJev and 66.7% for EEGNet (Supplementary Note 11). 7 Inference rules for known tasks and ordered-bin scores For tasks seen in training, averaging the log-probabilities of EEGJev and the ordinary classifier with equal weights gives 65.2% on test D1 and 63.2% on test D2. This is 1.4 points above EEGJev on D1 (+1.0 to +1.8) and 2.1 points on D2 (+1.4 to +2.9), and it is not distinguishable from EEGNet on D1 (+0.7, 0.5 to +1.9) or on D2 (+0.2, 1.3 to +1.6). Averaging and the full-label check were fixed before v1.3 test evaluation and applied to the saved test outputs without additional fitting (Supplementary Note 11). Both apply only to tasks with known training labels. Figure 5c,d shows D3 accuracy by task and mean error in bins. The D3 branch of EEGJev reaches 41.5% on test and EEGNet 42.5%, paired difference of 1.0 points (2.8 to +0.8). The bin heads of the ordinary classifier reach 42.4%. On the 14 D3 tasks covered by LaBraM, the D3 branch scores 34.0% and LaBraM 39.7% (Figure 4c). The mean bin distance is 0.80 for the D3 branch, 0.83 for the ordinary bin heads and 0.75 for EEGNet. On validation the branch is at 41.3% and EEGNet at 42.7%. Without the branch, the decision head answers D3 at 35.3% on test, 7.2 points below EEGNet (Supplementary Note 12), so the binned questions are matched only with the further-trained branch.

sections.title: Datasets no model has seen
sections.content: On left-or-right-hand motor imagery in two datasets that no model had been trained or evaluated on, Weibo2014 11 with 10 persons and Dreyer2023A 12 with 60, EEGJev stays at chance (49.6% to 52.4%). The ordinary classifier (53.1% to 58.1%) is above it in all six conditions, by 2.2 to 7.0 points with intervals that exclude zero. Supplementary Note 9 describes the setup and few-shot calibration.

sections.title: Response time for individual questions
sections.content: EEGJev and NeuroLM-B answered the same 192 binary D1 validation questions (Exo walking transitions and LEMON eye state) one at time, with checkpoints from three training seeds and 576 timed calls per model per platform. On one CPU core, the 95th-percentile response times were 394.97 ms for EEGJev and 3,677.34 ms for NeuroLM-B. On one GPU they were 9.60 and 24.99 ms, respectively. On each platform, EEGJev returned an offered option in all 576 calls and NeuroLM-B in 554. Timing started with preprocessed EEG in host memory, included text processing and answer return, and counted unparseable responses as infinite time to an offered option (Supplementary Note 6).

sections.title: Discussion
sections.content: EEGJev-Bench measures two decisions separately. Does the answer match the requested attribute, and is its value correct? On attribute pairs seen in training, EEGJev selected the requested attribute with 98.0% to 100% accuracy across 13 test sources. Balanced accuracy for the specific answer ranged from 40.2% to 85.0% (Figure 3a). Task-specific EEGNet achieved higher joint accuracy on paired questions, and EEGJevs refusal head outperformed EEGNets confidence rule. EEGJev scored the offered answers in one pass and had shorter 95th-percentile response time than NeuroLM-B on the same 192 validation questions answered individually, on both single CPU core and GPU. Golan et al. 13 used paired sentences to reveal failures that aggregate languagemodel scores could miss. Gu et al. 14 evaluated candidate selection in cardiac question answering, and EEGJev-Bench holds the EEG and answer choices fixed to test whether decoder follows change in the requested attribute. Most sources taken from UniEQA have one to three test participants. Bootstrap intervals over tasks condition on these participants. Validation is used for model selection or calibration, and the D1 gap between EEGJev and EEGNet is larger on validation than on test. The long-window result rests on 17 tasks from 8 sources, and the event times of T2 are instruction, cue or scoring times. The refusal head scores 59.2%, 9.2 percentage points above the 50% baseline for rule that ignores 10 the EEG. Letter codes in place of the candidate names bring EEGJev down to the level of the controls without EEG, so it depends on the wording of the candidates. The held-out task results cover one concept seen in other sources and one attribute that no other source asks, and they show that transfer is possible, not how often it occurs. The motor-imagery transfer fills missing electrodes by interpolation, and the training data contain only two persons who imagine left and right hand movements. The decision-head stage of EEGJev trains 806.8 million parameters. Baselines use the benchmarks splits and preprocessing. The fixed T1 and T2 rules combine D1 outputs. The supervised T2 readouts use the same T2 labels as EEGJev (Figure 6). METIS and LEAF use released weights. Comparisons with them involve differences in model design and training conditions. EEGJev lets users specify what to decode from an EEG recording through question and returns probability for each offered answer in one pass. EEGJevBench holds the recording fixed while varying the question or the availability of the correct option, so researchers can assess question following, answer accuracy and refusal separately.

sections.title: Methods
sections.content: EEGJev-Bench EEGJev-Bench asks multiple-choice questions about attributes such as the stimulus shown, the sleep stage or the participants diagnosis. All results use data version v1.3. Sources and windows We use recordings from the original releases of all 19 sources (Figure 2, Supplementary Note 1, Supplementary Table 1). For 12 sources from Unified_EQA, the public EEG question-answering release in UniEQA 15, we locate each of its segments in the original recording. The seven added sources are COG-BCI 16, HBN-EEG 17,18, verbal working memory dataset 19, the Dortmund Vital Study 20, ERP CORE 21, MPI-LEMON 22 and resting-state depression dataset 23. Seventeen sources have scored tasks. The bciciv and is sources have three training persons each and no test persons in this version, so they serve as training material only. Short windows last 1, 2 or 4 s. An event label gives one window from the event, and state or person label gives at most eight non-overlapping windows per segment. Long windows of 8, 16 or 30 are cut around an event for the T2 questions. All recordings come from public datasets, and no new data were recorded for this study. For 15 of the 19 sources, the original publications or dataset pages state an ethics approval and the consent of the participants. Those of BCI Competition IV, CHB-MIT and Sleep-EDF state neither, and those of the depression dataset state consent without naming review board. Question types D1 asks one attribute of one window. Its options are all train values of that attribute for the same source and window length, so they depend on the cell (source, attribute, window length) and not on the window. Each attribute has three phrasings, and D1 row uses one of them. Each attribute also has two phrasings that occur in no training text, and every D1 test row is repeated with both of them (D1h). 11 D2 asks two attributes of the same window, each in all three phrasings. The pair is chosen so that neither attribute determines the other over the train segments of the source. D2 is scored per attribute, and joint score counts window as correct only when both attributes are answered correctly. D3 asks the model to choose among ordered categories. The questions cover MMSE by clinical cut points ( 24, 1823, < 18), age in the Dortmund, HBN and LEMON sources, sleep stage by level (Wake, N1, N2, N3), n-back load, the level of the MATB task and the foreground contrast in HBN. During benchmark construction, we merged two LEMON age bins (5565 and 6570 years) after the test label counts showed that the younger bin was empty (Supplementary Note 2). D3 is scored by balanced accuracy and by the mean absolute distance between the chosen and the true bin. D4 tests refusal. For each D1 question with at least three options, D4 adds refusal row, in which the correct option is removed, and control row, in which one wrong option is removed and the correct answer remains. Both rows have one option fewer than the D1 question, so the number of options does not reveal the correct decision. T1 shows two windows of the same person and of the same length and asks which of them carries given label of D1 task. Each pair gives four linked views, with the two windows in either order and each of the two labels asked. window enters at most one pair of task. T2 asks whether an event lies in the first or the second half of long window. The event is placed near one quarter or three quarters of the window, with jitter of one sixteenth of its length, and the two placements of an event form one linked group. The events are changes of eye state, seizure onsets, sleep stage changes, cued transitions, changes of flicker frequency and targets in stimulus stream. Their labels are instruction, cue or scoring times, not measured neural onsets. The train and validation persons have 940,604 short windows and 6,728,339 D1 to D4 questions. The test persons have 117,571 short windows and 878,827 questions, and D1h adds 488,786 rows. The scored T1 tasks have 557,933 train pairs, 94,924 validation pairs and 80,748 test pairs, and the scored T2 tasks have 64,465, 12,315 and 3,368 event groups. Splits In the 17 scored sources, participants belong to only one split. For the seven added sources, 15% of the persons form the test split and 15% of the rest the validation split, drawn with fixed seeds. For the sources from UniEQA, test and validation persons were drawn with fixed seeds in the numbers of the earlier data version, so most of these sources have few test persons (ten for dementia and photo, three for asym and sleep, two for chbmit, mom, surprise and vrnf, one for exo and gal). Photo and dementia record the same participants and are split jointly. The added sources have between 4 test persons (cogbci) and 91 (dortmund). Results are therefore reported per task and with the number of test persons in mind. Data quality rules In study of six EEG datasets, changing preprocessing alone altered up to 42% of trial-level predictions 24. We use one signal pipeline to construct the benchmark windows. We read each recording from its original file using fixed channel list. For ERP CORE, we first subtract the mean across the 30 scalp channels at each time point. We apply notch filter at the mains frequency where peak is present, resample the whole recording to 200 Hz and standardize each channel within each 12 window. We exclude windows that start in the first 2 s, end in the last 0.5 s, lie within 0.1 of discontinuity marker or contain flat or dead channels. We correct labels against the original data, for example by restoring the official bciciv motor imagery labels and cutting each gal window from its own lift (Supplementary Note 2). Evaluation protocol Each row is scored with its own options in the given order. task is cell of one question type. The main metric of D1, D1h, D2 and D3 is balanced accuracy over answer labels, computed within each task. task is scored only if every offered answer has at least 10 windows on validation and on test, and this task list was fixed on 15 November 2026 from the label counts alone, before any model was trained on this data version. It has 109 D1 tasks in 17 sources, 59 D2 tasks in 10 sources, 22 D3 tasks in 6 sources and 31 D4 tasks in 11 sources. Scores are averaged with equal weight for every source and equal weight for the tasks within source (the sourcebalanced mean), so that source with many tasks does not dominate. D3 also reports the mean absolute bin distance. The D2 joint score averages the nine combinations of phrasings of window and is balanced over the combinations of the two answers. In the fixed-option experiment, we count question pair as correct only when both answers are correct and average the scores within each pairing condition, across conditions within each source and then across sources. D4 is scored by group-balanced criterion. group holds the D4 rows that share source, attribute, window length and the unordered set of offered labels. Within group, the criterion is the mean of the refusal recall on refusal rows and the answer rate on control rows, and tasks score is the mean over its groups that contain both kinds of rows. rule that does not look at the EEG cannot exploit which label is missing, since every decision that is constant within group scores exactly 0.5. Every model can refuse by thresholding its calibrated maximum option probability. Per model, one temperature is fitted on validation D1 by negative log-likelihood and one threshold, shared across sources, is chosen on validation D4. Models with their own refusal output are also scored with it. Calibration is reported as the expected calibration error over 15 bins (ECE) of the D1 answers after temperature scaling. T1 and T2 are scored by accuracy. The linked views of pair or an event group are averaged first, then persons, tasks and sources, so that the four views of pair do not count as four samples. T1 or T2 task is scored when validation and test each have at least ten pairs or event groups, which leaves 93 T1 tasks in 16 sources and 17 T2 tasks in 8 sources. Chance is 50% for both. Controls without EEG Three controls receive no information from the EEG of the window being asked about (an answer prior, text-only Laya checkpoint 10 and shuffled EEG). On D1 they reach 43.5% to 43.8% on validation and test, the level of the answer prior (Supplementary Note 3, Supplementary Table 2).

sections.title: EEGJev
sections.content: EEGJev answers multiple-choice question about EEG. It receives one window, or two windows for T1, the question text and the offered candidates. It returns one score per candidate and, from separate output, whether it should refuse. The candidate set can change at run time, and nothing is generated or parsed (Figure 1). 13 EEG encoder. The encoder is CBraMod 2 with the official pretrained weights. It reads each sources native channels at 200 Hz in patches of one second, so window of channels and seconds gives tokens of width 200. In first step, one encoder is fine-tuned on the D1 labels of all 19 sources together. Each source and window length has its own hidden layers, namely the two-layer head that CBraMod places on the flattened tokens (200CL to 800 to 200 units, with ELU and dropout 0.1), and each cell has its own linear output layer. The encoder is then frozen. The same step-1 model with its per-cell output layers is the ordinary classifier described in Baselines. Decision head. The decision head is small bidirectional transformer that reads one sequence per question. The sequence holds the windows CBraMod tokens, one spatial token, and the text tokens of the question and of each candidate. Each CBraMod token is projected to width 256 and receives channel and patch embedding. The spatial token summarizes the whole window. New hidden layers of the same shape as the step-1 heads, one set per source and window length, map the flattened CBraMod tokens to 200 units, and linear layer and learned embedding turn the result into one more token. CBraMod has no vocabulary, so the text is read by frozen MPNet encoder (all-mpnet-base-v2 8), whose 768-dimensional token outputs are projected to width 256. Segment and question-type embeddings mark which part of the sequence position belongs to, and each candidate has marker position. The head has two pre-norm layers with four attention heads, feed-forward width of 1,024 and dropout 0.1. Every position attends to every other position, so each candidate is scored in the context of the others. two-layer scorer reads each marker and returns the candidates logit, and softmax over the offered candidates gives the answer probabilities. This joint scoring of candidates at markers follows the typed decision model Laya 10. EEGJev uses none of Layas weights. Two windows and long windows. The same head answers T1 and T2. For T1, the tokens of both windows enter the sequence, and learned embedding marks each token as belonging to window or window B. The two candidates name the windows, and the tokens of candidate attend to the EEG tokens of its own window only. For T2, the long window is cut into consecutive blocks of at most 4 (1 for erpcore, which has hidden layers for 1 only), the frozen encoder reads each block separately with the hidden layers of its source and length, and learned embedding gives the position of each block. The tokens of the candidate for the first half attend to the EEG tokens of the blocks in the first half only, and likewise for the second half. block that spans the midpoint belongs to both halves. No new encoder layers are added for long windows. The decision-head stage trains 806.8 million parameters. Its 52 sets of spatialtoken hidden layers contain 804.7 million (99.74%), and its two transformer layers together contain 1.58 million. With the frozen CBraMod and MPNet, EEGJev is therefore not small model (Supplementary Note 6). Refusal output. separate Act head decides whether to answer. It is two-layer network (260 to 256 to 2 units) that reads the first output position of the decision head and four features of the answer distribution, namely the top probability, the gap between the top two 14 probabilities, the entropy divided by log and the number of offered candidates divided by 255. EEGJev refuses when the Act heads refusal output is the larger of its two outputs. Training. With the encoder frozen, one decision head is trained on all question types except D3 and D4. The 3,258,618 D1 and D2 questions of the training persons are used for 18,900 updates of 64 questions with soft cross-entropy over the offered candidates. Options are shuffled, 25% of the questions offer random subset of their options, and 10% replace the option texts by letters whose mapping is stated in the question. For D1 question whose source asks another attribute at the same window length, quarter of the draws offer the labels of both attributes together, so that the question decides which attribute is asked. Mixed into the same schedule are 10,463 updates on T1 pairs and 1,913 updates on T2 event groups, 31,276 updates in all. The Act head is trained afterwards, with the decision head frozen, on pairs of D4 training rows, to refuse on refusal rows and to answer on control rows. The decision head sees no D3 questions, and its own D3 balanced accuracy is 34.1% on validation. D3 branch therefore continues from the trained head on D3 training questions mixed with D1 and D2 questions and answers the D3 rows only. All D1, D2, D4, T1 and T2 results use the main head. Three seeds are trained, and each seed has its own step-1 encoder. Supplementary Note 4 summarizes the training schedule.

sections.title: Experimental setup
sections.content: Baselines Baselines use the benchmarks windows, splits and scorer on the tasks they cover. Paired comparisons use rows that both models score. These scores describe performance under our benchmark protocol. EEGNet 25 and LaBraM 1 are trained for each D1 and D3 task. LaBraM has no models for chbmit, hbn and sleep, whose channels its channel table does not cover. The ordinary classifier is EEGJevs step-1 model (see EEGJev). It does not read the question. These three answer D2 row with the model or output layer for the requested attribute. The default D4 refusal rule uses confidence threshold. We report the full-label check separately where available. Three baselines read the question. NeuroLM 3 is instruction-tuned on the D1 and D2 training questions of the benchmark without text-only batches, followed by short stage on D3 questions, and has no input for hbn and sleep. METIS 5 and LEAF 4 are run from their released checkpoints without training on the benchmark. METIS scores the option letters in one forward pass. LEAF covers 12 of the 17 scored sources and is reported at its three instruction levels. As comparison rows, we also build the ordinary classifier and EEGJev on per-source encoders. Supplementary Note 5 describes the training and inference settings. The fixed comparisons in Figure 6 combine each baselines D1 outputs without fitting to T1 or T2 labels. For T1, the composed answer is the window to which the models D1 output gives the higher probability of the asked label. For T2, the models one-second D1 output is computed on every consecutive second of the long window. For change of state, the answer is the half that holds the second at which the mean output before and after differs most, and for target in stream it is the half that holds the second with the highest target probability. The photo events have no matching D1 attribute, so 15 of the 17 T2 tasks can be composed. These 15 rules were fixed before any model output existed. The same compositions applied to EEGJevs own D1 answers serve as control. For the supervised T2 comparison, we kept the one-second EEGNet and shared ordinary classifiers frozen and fitted logistic regression for each task and seed. The input was either the class probabilities concatenated in time order or their mean across the window. We standardized each feature using the training split and selected the inverse regularization strength (C = 0.01, 0.1, 1 or 10) on validation, choosing the smaller value in tie. The selected readouts were then applied to the test split. Protocol The tables average three seeds for each trained model. We use validation for checkpoint selection where applicable and to fit temperatures and D4 thresholds. NeuroLM uses the checkpoint after its final 300-step stage (Supplementary Note 5). The model, training recipe, task list and primary metrics were frozen before the v1.3 test. Further v1.3 analyses include fixed-option question switching, participant and source resampling, supervised T2 readouts and full-label refusal rescoring. Supplementary Notes 12, 11 and 14 describe D3 head scores, averaging and the paired D4 comparisons. Most of the earlier sources have few test participants (see Splits). Differences between models are computed per task on the rows that every model in the comparison scored. They are given as the source-balanced mean of the paired task differences with 95% interval from bootstrap over tasks within sources (10,000 resamples). These task-based intervals condition on the participants evaluated. For the D1 comparison of EEGJev and EEGNet, we also computed paired 95% percentile interval from 10,000 resamples of participants within sources, keeping each participants windows together across both models and all three seeds. The same draw was used for participants shared by dementia and photo. For matched T2 readouts, we also used 10,000 paired resamples to estimate intervals. One analysis resampled participants with matched T2 data within fixed sources. The other resampled sources first and then drew participants from each selected sources test pool. Both placements of an event stayed with their participant. The scores in the tables are each models own source-balanced means over the tasks it covers, so they can differ slightly from the paired differences. Supplementary Note 6 reports model sizes and response times.

Supplementary Note 4. Training details of EEGJev Step 1. We fine-tuned for 50 epochs and kept the checkpoint with the highest mean validation balanced accuracy over cells. Decision head. Over 50 epochs, we sampled sources in proportion to the square root of their question counts and window lengths in proportion to their counts. We weighted questions by inverse answer frequency within each cell and kept both questions from each D2 window together. D1 draws offering two attributes used up to 12 options and omitted the subset and letter augmentations. We used 557,933 T1 training pairs and 64,465 T2 training event groups. Each sampled pair or group contributed one linked view under the same sampling weights. We selected the checkpoint on D1 and D2 validation questions, with up to 300 per task. Act and D3 heads. The frozen decision head supplied features to the Act head, which used up to 2,000 D4 pairs per cell for 11 epochs of 788 updates with 64 rows each. Pairs from 15% of training windows were held out for epoch selection. The D3 branch continued from the trained head for six epochs of 400 updates, with each batch split evenly between D3 questions and pool of D1 and D2 questions. Supplementary Note 5.
